title: Quanto custa? — numbers, prices and cafés
goal: Count to a thousand, ask prices, order at a café and pay — while meeting a few numbers that are **spelled differently** in Portugal and in Brazil.
bekal: ask *Quanto custa?* and understand the answer
order at a café with the phrases the Portuguese really use

dialogs.title: Diálogo — Na pastelaria
dialogs.intro: At four in the afternoon, Budi walks into a small *pastelaria* — a pastry shop and café — near his house.

lines.speaker: Empregado:
lines.id: Good afternoon! What can I get you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Um café e um pastel de nata, se faz favor.
lines.id: A coffee and a pastel de nata, please.
lines.literal: a coffee and a pastry of cream, if makes favor.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Sim, uma água sem gás. Quanto é tudo?
lines.id: Yes, a still water. How much is everything?
lines.literal: yes, a water without gas. how-much is all?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Aqui está. Tem troco de vinte?
lines.id: Here you are. Do you have change for a twenty?
lines.literal: here it-is. has change of twenty?

lines.speaker: Empregado:
lines.text: Tenho, sim. Aqui está: dezasseis e oitenta.
lines.id: I do. Here you go: sixteen eighty.
lines.literal: I-have, yes. here it-is: sixteen and eighty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Obrigado. O café aqui é muito bom.
lines.id: Thanks. The coffee here is really good.
lines.literal: obliged. the coffee here is very good.

lines.speaker: Empregado:
lines.text: É o melhor da rua! Quantos cafés bebe por dia?
lines.id: Best on the street! How many coffees do you drink a day?
lines.literal: is the best of-the street! how-many coffees drinks per day?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Três ou quatro. Em Portugal bebo mais.
lines.id: Three or four. In Portugal I drink more.
lines.literal: three or four. in Portugal I-drink more.

notes: **Faz favor and se faz favor** are Portugal's way of saying "go ahead" and "please". Staff use it to ask "what can I get you?", customers use it as "please". It's also the polite way to call a waiter from across the room: just say *Se faz favor!* — don't wave. *Por favor* is also correct and better known outside Portugal.

**São três euros, but É um euro.** The verb follows the amount: if the price is more than one, use *são*; if it's exactly one, use *é*. Cents are read as a plain number after *e*: *três euros e vinte* = €3.20. The Portuguese write it 3,20 € — with a decimal comma, where English uses a point.

**Dezasseis, not dezesseis.** Four numbers are spelled differently in Portugal: *dezasseis* (16), *dezassete* (17), *dezanove* (19), and *catorze* (14, which in Brazil can also be *quatorze*). Note the **a** in the middle — this is the Portuguese spelling, and the one used throughout this course.

**Um café in Portugal means an espresso**, not a big mug of coffee. Order *um café* in Lisbon and a tiny cup of strong black coffee arrives. In Lisbon it's also called *uma bica*; in Porto, *um cimbalino*. If you want a big milky coffee in a glass, order *um galão*.
**Tem troco de vinte?** — *troco* is change. This question is very useful, because many small shops in Portugal are reluctant to take big notes for small purchases.
**Bom apetite** is said to anyone eating or about to eat, even strangers at the next table. The reply: *Obrigado, igualmente.*

grammars.title: Numbers 0 to 20
body: Only two of them change for gender: **um/uma** and **dois/duas**. The rest stay the same.
after: *Duas* is used with feminine nouns: *duas horas*, *duas casas*, *duas irmãs*. This is one of the most common beginner mistakes, because the other numbers don't change, which makes it easy to forget that this one does.
The numbers in bold are the four with a typically Portuguese spelling.

grammars.title: Tens, hundreds, thousands
body: Compound numbers are joined with **e** ("and") — everywhere, not just in one spot as in British "one hundred and five".
after: **Cem is exactly 100; cento is for 101 and up.** *Cem euros* (100), but *cento e vinte euros* (120). It's the only number with two forms like this.
**Hundreds agree in gender:** *duzentos livros* but *duzentas casas*. Likewise *trezentos/trezentas*, *quinhentos/quinhentas*. Tens never change.
*Mil* is never preceded by *um*: just *mil euros*, not *um mil euros*.

blocks.text: *Ficar com* literally means "to stay with", and it's used exactly like "I'll take it" when you decide to buy something. The verb *ficar* is extremely productive in Portugal — it also means "to be located" (*Onde fica a estação?*) and "to become" (*fico contente*).

blocks.title: Two small things that make you sound local
items: The Portuguese drink their coffee **standing at the counter**, not sitting — and it's often cheaper that way. Say your order straight out, without a long preamble: *Um café, se faz favor.*
*Sumo* means juice in Portugal; in Brazil it's *suco*. And an *imperial* is a small draft beer in Lisbon — in Porto the same thing is called a *fino*.
The plural of *pastel* is **pastéis**: *dois pastéis de nata*. Remember the *-l → -is* rule from Unit 2.
